newsitem.title: UK: British government hails flying start in 100 days.
newsitem.headline: British government hails flying start in 100 days.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government, basking in a run of excellent opinion poll ratings, boasted on Friday that it had made a "cracking start" in its first 100 days in office.
But the deputy prime minister, John Prescott, told a news conference ministers were celebrating Saturday's landmark, "without any sense of complacency".

The celebrations were in order according to a Gallup poll published in the Daily Telegraph which showed an 83 percent approval rating for Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is currently on holiday in Italy.

This was far higher than the figures achieved by other prime ministers after three months in office. His nearest rival since polling began was the post-World War Two Labour prime minister, Clement Attlee, who had a 66 percent rating at the same stage.

The poll, conducted between July 31 and August 6, showed 58 percent support for Labour, down three percentage points from a month earlier, but 13 points higher than they achieved at the May 1 election which swept them to power with a 179-seat parliamentary majority.
"We have made a cracking start, but there is a long way to go," Prescott said. "Our contract is for five years, and we will implement it." British parliamentary terms are a maximum of five years.

Peter Mandelson, a key adviser to Blair and a minister without portfolio, was also cautious about the longer term. "People are happy with the start we have made, but it is only the end of the beginning," he told the news conference.

Labour published a "100 days, 100 achievements" document to emphasise what it had done to honour the five key commitments on which it won the election, ending 18 consecutive years of rule by its Conservative opponents.

It said it had moved to cut class sizes in primary schools, put more resources into treating National Health Service patients, launched a scheme to help the young unemployed into work, speeded up criminal justice and honoured its pledge not to raise income tax.
The government received a further endorsement from the world of business when Britain's Institute of Management published a poll of members' views of the first 100 days of office.

Giving ministers six out of 10 for their efforts after analysing the poll, the Institute's director general, Roger Young, said: "While gold stars may be absent from the report card, the silvers are solid."
The last two weeks of the government's first hundred days have seen a series of controversies and setbacks which have led commentators to question whether the Blair honeymoon is about to end.

The Conservatives increased their winning margin in a parliamentary by-election in the west London constituency of Uxbridge on July 31, and made political capital out of a minister's initial refusal to sell two million pounds worth of shares in British Petroleum, claiming a possible conflict of interest.
Meanwhile, the suicide of a Scottish Labour MP has saddened the party, and Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has announced he is leaving his wife of 28 years for his secretary in parliament.

On Thursday, British commercial bank base interest rates went up by a quarter of a percentage point for the fourth time since Labour took office in a bid to dampen a consumer boom. They now stand at seven percent, the highest since 1992.

The centre-left New Statesman political weekly warned in its latest edition: "The grey cumulus of autumn is already taking shape on the horizon. Sterling is seriously overvalued and the higher interest rates needed to cool the consumer economy may well make matters worse."
